title: TKDL Prior Art Formulation: Ashwagandhadi Churna (Charaka Samhita)
source: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - CSIR / Ministry of Ayush
text:
TKDL Identifier: CSIR-TKDL-AY-2001-001.
Classical Source: Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana, Adhyaya 2 (Vajikarana Adhyaya).
System of Medicine: Ayurveda.
Formulation: Ashwagandhadi Churna.
Ingredients: Ashwagandha root (Withania somnifera), Vidarikanda tuber (Pueraria tuberosa), Shatavari root (Asparagus racemosus), processed with Goghrita (cow ghee).
Traditional Indication: Balya (strength promoting), Rasayana (rejuvenator), and Dhatuposhaka (nourishment of body tissues).
Patent Prior Art Significance: This classical composition is established prior art under Section 3(p) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970. Any patent application claiming a simple herbal mixture of Ashwagandha with Shatavari and Vidari without unexpected synergistic bioassay proof is liable to be rejected based on this TKDL record. CSIR-TKDL access agreements with USPTO, EPO, and JPO allow patent examiners to cite this reference as anticipatory prior art.

title: TKDL Prior Art Formulation: Haridra Khanda (Bhaishajya Ratnavali)
source: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - CSIR / Ministry of Ayush
text:
TKDL Identifier: CSIR-TKDL-AY-2002-089.
Classical Source: Bhaishajya Ratnavali, Sheetapitta Chikitsa Prakarana.
System of Medicine: Ayurveda.
Formulation: Haridra Khanda (Brihat).
Ingredients: Pure Rhizome powder of Haridra (Curcuma longa), fried in cow ghee (Go-Ghrita), boiled with milk (Godugdha) and sugar candy, fortified with Trikatu (Sunthi, Maricha, Pippali), Trijataka (Twak, Ela, Patra), and Vidanga.
Traditional Indication: Sheetapitta (urticaria), Udarda (allergic skin lesions), Kandu (pruritus), and Kotha (erythema).
Patent Defense Context: Following the revocation of the US Turmeric Patent (US Patent 5,401,504) by CSIR, this formulation was systematically indexed in TKDL. Claims for using turmeric extracts with black pepper (piperine) for anti-allergic or anti-inflammatory conditions are directly anticipated by this classical record under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 unless non-obvious nanocarrier delivery or unexpected synergy is clinically established.

title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India: Withania somnifera Monograph
authority: Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy (PCIM&H)
rule: Second Schedule of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
text:
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API), Part I, Vol I, Monograph 12.
Canonical Drug: Ashwagandha (Dry root of Withania somnifera Dunal, family Solanaceae).
Synonyms: Sanskrit: Hayagandha, Vajigandha, Balada; Hindi: Asgandh; Telugu: Asvagandha, Pennerugadda; Tamil: Amukkarakizhangu.
Macroscopic Characters: Roots straight, unbranched, conical, tortuous, 10 to 20 cm long, 10 to 20 mm thick, outer surface buff to grey-yellow with longitudinal wrinkles.
Identity & Quantitative Standards:
- Foreign Matter: Not more than 2 per cent.
- Total Ash: Not more than 7 per cent.
- Acid-insoluble Ash: Not more than 1 per cent.
- Alcohol-soluble Extractive: Not less than 15 per cent.
- Water-soluble Extractive: Not less than 19 per cent.
- Total Withanolides (Assay by HPLC): Not less than 0.20 per cent w/w calculated on dry root basis.
Regulatory Mandate: Under the Second Schedule to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, compliance with API monographs is legally mandatory for any licensed Ayurvedic drug manufacturer in India.

title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India: Tinospora cordifolia (Guduchi) Monograph
authority: Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy (PCIM&H)
rule: Second Schedule of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940
text:
Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API), Part I, Vol I, Monograph 24.
Canonical Drug: Guduchi (Dry stem of Tinospora cordifolia (Willd.) Miers, family Menispermaceae).
Synonyms: Sanskrit: Amrita, Chhinnaruha, Chakralakshana; Hindi: Giloy; Telugu: Tippateega; Tamil: Seenthilkodi.
Macroscopic Standards: Cylindrical pieces, 1 to 5 cm diameter, greenish-brown surface with prominent lenticels and longitudinal fissures; wheel-like vascular bundles in transverse section.
Physicochemical Parameters:
- Foreign Organic Matter: Not more than 2 per cent.
- Total Ash: Not more than 8 per cent.
- Acid-insoluble Ash: Not more than 0.5 per cent.
- Alcohol-soluble Extractive: Not less than 3 per cent.
- Water-soluble Extractive: Not less than 11 per cent.
- Bitters content / TLC Fingerprint matching marker compound cordifolioside A and tinocordiside.
Enforceability: Standard binding on all Ayurvedic formulations containing Giloy/Guduchi as per Section 33EEB of Drugs & Cosmetics Act 1940.

title: Ayurvedic Formulary of India: Triphala Churna Specification
text:
Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI), Part I, Formulation 7:13.
Canonical Formulation: Triphala Churna.
Classical Reference: Sharangadhara Samhita, Madhyama Khanda, Adhyaya 6: 9-11.
Formulation Composition:
1. Haritaki fruit pericarp (Terminalia chebula Retz.) - 1 Part (Equal proportion).
2. Bibhitaki fruit pericarp (Terminalia bellirica Roxb.) - 1 Part (Equal proportion).
3. Amalaki fruit pericarp (Phyllanthus emblica L.) - 1 Part (Equal proportion).
Method of Preparation: De-seeded pericarps of mature fruits are dried, individually pulverized to fine powder (passing through mesh sieve 80), and blended uniformly in equal parts.
Dosage Form & Dosage: Churna (fine powder), 3 g to 6 g once or twice daily with warm water or honey.
Indications: Vibandha (constipation), Deepana (carminative), Netraroga (eye disorders), and Rasayana (antioxidant tonic).
Patent Law Relevance: Under Section 3(e) of the Indian Patents Act, any patent application seeking protection for an equal-ratio combination of Haritaki, Bibhitaki, and Amalaki is rejected as an unpatentable mere admixture of traditionally known ingredients unless an inventive extraction step and synergistic pharmacological effect is proven.

title: Ayurvedic Formulary of India: Chyawanprash Avaleha Standard
rule: First Schedule to Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940
text:
Ayurvedic Formulary of India (AFI), Part I, Formulation 3:11.
Canonical Formulation: Chyawanprash (Avaleha).
Classical Reference: Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana, Adhyaya 1:1, Sloka 62-74.
Key Ingredients: Fresh Amalaki fruits (500 pieces), decoction of Dashamoola and associated herbs (36 herbs), fried in cow ghee and sesame oil, enriched with sugar syrup, bamboo manna (Vamshalochana), long pepper (Pippali), cardamom (Ela), and raw honey.
Dosage & Therapeutic Use: 12 g to 24 g daily with milk. Indicated for Kasa (cough), Shwasa (dyspnoea), Kshaya (wasting), and Rasayana (immune rejuvenation).
Regulatory Distinction: Governed under the First Schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Manufacturers marketing Chyawanprash under classical names cannot claim proprietary patent rights under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970.

title: The Patents Act, 1970: Section 3(e) - Exclusion of Mere Admixtures
source: India Code - Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
authority: Parliament of India / Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
text:
The Patents Act, 1970 (Act No. 39 of 1970), Chapter II, Section 3(e).
Statutory Text:
Section 3. What are not inventions — The following are not inventions within the meaning of this Act,—
(e) a substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof or a process for producing such substance.

Statutory Interpretation for Ayurvedic and Herbal Innovations:
Under Indian Patent Office (IPO) Guidelines for Examination of Patent Applications in the Field of Pharmaceuticals and Traditional Knowledge:
1. When an applicant combines known medicinal herbs or extract fractions (such as Ashwagandha and Brahmi), the objection under Section 3(e) is mandatory.
2. To overcome this statutory bar, the applicant MUST submit comparative in-vitro bioassay or clinical pharmacological data proving unexpected SYNERGY (where the therapeutic activity of the mixture is statistically significantly higher than the sum of its individual parts).
3. If no quantitative synergy data is submitted in the complete specification (Form 2), the application will be refused under Section 15.

title: The Patents Act, 1970: Section 3(p) - Exclusion of Traditional Knowledge
source: India Code - Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
text:
The Patents Act, 1970, Section 3(p) (as inserted by Act 38 of 2002).
Statutory Text:
Section 3. What are not inventions —
(p) an invention which in effect, is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components.

Examination Procedure:
- Patent examiners routinely conduct automated cross-searches against the CSIR-AYUSH Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).
- If the claimed formulation, combination, or use is documented in classical texts of Ayurveda, Unani, or Siddha, the invention is barred under Section 3(p).
- Patentability can only be recognized if the applicant proves an inventive step beyond traditional knowledge (such as a novel standardized bioactive isolation process, a non-obvious drug delivery vehicle like phytosomes or nanoparticles, or a validated new therapeutic indication not disclosed in ancient texts).

title: The Patents Act, 1970: Section 10(4)(ii)(D) - Disclosure of Biological Source and Origin
source: India Code - Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
text:
The Patents Act, 1970, Chapter III, Section 10(4)(ii)(D).
Statutory Requirement:
Where an invention uses biological material, the applicant must disclose the source and geographical origin of the biological material in the complete specification (Form 2).

Consequences of Non-Disclosure or False Disclosure:
1. Ground of Opposition: Under Section 25(1)(j) and Section 25(2)(j), failure to disclose or wrongful disclosure of the geographical origin of biological material is a ground for pre-grant and post-grant opposition.
2. Ground of Revocation: Under Section 64(1)(p), a granted patent is liable to be revoked by the High Court if the complete specification does not disclose or wrongly mentions the source or geographical origin of biological materials.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EE - Misbranded Ayurvedic Drugs
source: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (Act No. 23 of 1940)
authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) & Ministry of Ayush
chapter: Chapter IV-A: Provisions Relating to Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani Drugs
text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, Chapter IV-A, Section 33EE.
Statutory Definition of Misbranded Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani Drugs:
An Ayurvedic drug shall be deemed to be misbranded:—
(a) if it is so coloured, coated, powdered or polished that damage is concealed, or if it is made to appear of better or greater therapeutic value than it really is;
(b) if it is not labelled in the prescribed manner; or
(c) if its label or container or anything accompanying the drug bears any statement, design or device which makes any false claim for the drug or which is false or misleading in any particular.

Regulatory Enforceability: Selling, stocking, or manufacturing a misbranded Ayurvedic drug is an offence punishable under Section 33-I with imprisonment and fine.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940: Section 33EEB - Patent or Proprietary Ayurvedic Medicine Definition
authority: Ministry of Ayush / State Licensing Authorities
text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, Chapter IV-A, Section 33EEB.
Statutory Definition:
'Patent or Proprietary medicine' in relation to Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani systems means a drug which is a remedy or prescription presented in a form ready for internal or external administration of human beings or animals and which is not included in the edition of the authoritative books specified in the First Schedule, but contains as ingredients only substances included in those books or the Pharmacopoeias.

Key Legal Implications:
1. Unlike a patent granted under the Patents Act 1970, an Ayurvedic 'Patent or Proprietary Medicine' under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act is merely a regulatory licensing category, not a monopoly patent right.
2. All ingredients must be strictly sourced from texts listed in the First Schedule to the Act.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945: Rule 158B - Guidelines for Issue of License with Respect to ASU Drugs
authority: Ministry of Ayush / State Licensing Authorities
chapter: Part XVI: Manufacture for Sale of ASU Drugs
text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, Part XVI, Rule 158B.
Regulatory Mandate for Patent or Proprietary ASU Medicines:
For the grant of a manufacturing license (Form 25D) for Ayurvedic Patent or Proprietary medicines, applicants must submit:
Category A (Classical ingredients with new indication or dosage):
- Published literature / textual references from First Schedule texts.
- Acute oral toxicity data.
Category B (New combination of classical ingredients):
- Safety data: Acute oral toxicity studies as per OECD guidelines.
- Proof of Efficacy: Evidence from published peer-reviewed journals or a pilot clinical trial conducted by a recognized clinical research organization.
Category C (Aqueous/hydroalcoholic extracts of classical ingredients):
- Heavy metal testing, pesticide residue testing, microbial load compliance, and batch standardization data.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945: Schedule T - Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) for ASU Drugs
text:
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, Schedule T (Good Manufacturing Practices for ASU Drugs).
Mandatory Requirements for Every ASU Drug Factory:
1. Location and Surroundings: Factory must be situated in hygienic conditions, free from open drains or contaminants.
2. Minimum Manufacturing Space: Standard minimum area prescribed for churna, tablet/vati, taila/ghrita, and asava/arishta sections.
3. Quality Control Section: Must maintain an in-house laboratory or tie-up with a government-approved laboratory for raw material identity testing, moisture content, total ash, microbial load, and heavy metal testing.
4. Batch Manufacturing Records (BMR): Retention of batch samples and complete manufacturing records for a minimum of 3 years.
5. Compliance is a prerequisite for Form 26D GMP Certificate.

title: IP India Patent Publication: Synergistic Herbal Formulation for Metabolic Disorders
source: Indian Patent Office (IP India) Official Journal
authority: Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
text:
Indian Patent Number: IN 312450 (Application No. 201611012345).
Title: A Synergistic Standardized Phyto-Pharmaceutical Composition for Management of Glycemic Index.
Classification: IPC: A61K 36/9066, A61K 36/42, A61P 3/10.
Applicant: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR).
Overcoming Section 3(e) Examination:
The Patent Office initially issued an objection under Section 3(e) alleging mere admixture of turmeric and bitter gourd.
Applicant's Evidence of Synergy:
- Quantitative isobologram analysis and Combination Index (CI) calculation.
- At an extract ratio of 3:2:0.5 (Curcuma : Momordica : Piperine), glucose uptake in L6 myotubes increased by 214%, compared to 78% for Curcuma alone and 62% for Momordica alone (CI = 0.48 < 1.0, establishing strong pharmacological synergism).
Claim 1 (Granted): A synergistic oral composition comprising 45-55% w/w standardized curcuminoids, 30-40% charantin-enriched fraction, and 5% piperine, demonstrating Combination Index < 0.6.

title: Geographical Indications Registry: Kashmir Saffron (Application No. 635)
text:
Geographical Indications Registry of India, GI Application No. 635, Registration Certificate No. 372.
Registered Name: Kashmir Saffron.
Geographical Area: Karewas (Karewa highlands) of Jammu & Kashmir (districts of Pulwama, Budgam, Kishtwar, and Srinagar).
Product Description & Uniqueness:
- Kashmir Saffron (Crocus sativus Kashmiriana) is the only saffron in the world grown at an altitude of 1,600 m to 1,800 m above MSL.
- Chemical uniqueness: Exceptional concentration of Crocin (responsible for deep red color, >8.72%), Safranal (aroma, >32%), and Picrocrocin (bitterness, >5.6%).
Ayurvedic & IPR Significance:
- Used classical drug Kumkuma in Ayurveda (Charaka Samhita: Varnya, Raktaprasadana).
- Authorized users registered under the GI Act 1999 enjoy statutory protection against counterfeit branding under Section 21.

title: WIPO Intergovernmental Committee: Protection of Traditional Knowledge Draft Articles
authority: WIPO Intergovernmental Committee on IP and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC)
text:
WIPO Document WIPO/GRTKF/IC/47/4 (2023).
Title: Consolidated Text on the Protection of Traditional Knowledge.
Key Principles for Patent Offices Worldwide:
1. Prevention of Erroneous Patents: Contracting parties shall ensure that patent examiners verify traditional knowledge prior art before granting claims over genetic resources and associated medical knowledge.
2. Role of TKDL: Recognized India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) as the global gold standard for defensive disclosure preventing biopiracy.
3. Mandatory Disclosure Requirement: Recommends national patent laws mandate the disclosure of country of origin of biological materials and proof of Prior Informed Consent (PIC) under the Nagoya Protocol.

title: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda: Core Concepts & Botanical Standards
source: World Health Organization (WHO) Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine Unit
text:
WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda (2023).
Concept ID: WHO-AYUR-0412 — Rasayana (रसायन / రసాయన / ரசாயனம்).
Definition: A specialized branch and pharmacological action in Ayurveda aimed at conserving, rejuvenating, and strengthening body tissues (Dhatus), promoting longevity, enhancing mental competence (Medha), and imparting disease resistance (Vyadhikshamatva).
Standardized Multilingual Equivalents:
- Sanskrit: Rasāyana (रसायन)
- English: Rejuvenation therapy / Adaptogenic bio-immunomodulation
- Telugu: రసాయనం (Rasayanamu)
- Tamil: ரசாயனம் (Rasayanam)
- Hindi: रसायन (Rasayan)
Regulatory Relevance: Claims on product labels regarding 'Rasayana' effects are classified under Ayurvedic drug pharmacology; under FSSAI Ayurveda Aahara regulations, label claims must restrict terminology to dietary wellness without alleging reversal of degenerative pathology.

title: National Biodiversity Authority: Guidelines for Prior Approval under Section 6 of Biological Diversity Act
source: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) - Statutory Body of Govt. of India
text:
Biological Diversity Act, 2002, Section 6(1) & NBA Guidelines.
Mandatory Statutory Requirement:
No person shall apply for any intellectual property right, by whatever name called, in or outside India for any invention based on any research or information on a biological resource obtained from India without obtaining the prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA).

Form III Procedure & Timing:
1. Indian Applicants: May apply for patent first in India, but MUST obtain NBA approval before the grant of the patent.
2. Foreign Applicants / Entities with foreign equity: Must obtain prior approval before filing the patent application.
3. Application Form: Form III (Application for seeking prior approval of NBA for applying for intellectual property right).
4. Fee: Statutory fee of Rs. 500 per application.
5. Benefit Sharing Agreement: NBA executes an agreement stipulating benefit sharing (typically 0.2% to 1.0% of ex-factory gross sales if commercialized) into the National Biodiversity Fund.

title: Guidelines on Access to Biological Resources and Associated Knowledge and Benefits Sharing Regulations, 2014
source: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change / NBA Notification
text:
Guidelines on Access to Biological Resources and Associated Knowledge and Benefits Sharing Regulations, 2014 (S.O. 3013(E)).
Regulation 9: Criteria for Benefit Sharing for Commercial Utilization of Biological Resources:
1. Option A (Based on purchase price of biological resource):
   - When buyer purchases directly from gatherers/cultivators: 1.0% to 3.0% of the purchase price.
   - When purchased through traders: 3.0% to 5.0% of the purchase price.
2. Option B (Based on annual gross ex-factory sale of product):
   - Up to Rupees 1 Crore: 0.1 per cent.
   - Rupees 1 Crore to 3 Crores: 0.2 per cent.
   - Above Rupees 3 Crores: 0.5 per cent.
3. IPR Commercialization: In case of patent transfer / licensing to a third party, the patentee must pay 3.0% to 5.0% of the royalty or licensing fee received.
